sources.claim: Turing's 1950 paper "Computing Machinery and Intelligence" (Mind) proposed replacing "Can machines think?" with an imitation game in which an interrogator questions a hidden human and a machine; the test is debated, and the name is sometimes used loosely for any behavioral test.

"A Proposal for the Dartmouth Summer Research Project on Artificial Intelligence" (dated August 31, 1955; McCarthy, Minsky, Rochester, Shannon) proposed a 1956 workshop and is credited with introducing the term "artificial intelligence".

questions.intro: Two early moments shaped how people talk about AI. In 1950, Alan Turing's paper "Computing Machinery and Intelligence" asked whether machines could think and proposed the imitation game as a practical test. In August 1955, John McCarthy, Marvin Minsky, Nathaniel Rochester and Claude Shannon wrote a proposal for a summer research project at Dartmouth College in 1956; the proposal is credited with introducing the term "ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE." These moments matter because they framed AI as a research field and set questions people still debate.

questions.prompt: How optimistic was the Dartmouth proposal?

choices.text: It suggested significant progress in one summer

questions.correct_answer: It suggested significant progress in one summer
questions.intro: Early researchers were very optimistic: the Dartmouth proposal suggested significant progress could be made in one summer by a small group. Progress turned out to be much slower and uneven, with periods of reduced funding and interest. Remembering this helps when reading today's confident predictions. History also shows that a name can shape expectations: "intelligence" invites comparisons with people that the systems may not support.
